title: Chicken Pilau
author: Maama Nakato
desc: Chicken browned in pilau and chicken masala then lifted out, potatoes cooked nearly dry in tomato, everything returned with the rice, a litre of hot water poured in — and then the lid goes on and you do not stir at all.
longDesc: This is the absorption pilau, and it is built in a strict order for a reason. The chicken browns in the spices and comes straight back out, so it does not overcook while the rice does. The potatoes and tomatoes reduce until fairly dry. Then rice, chicken, grated carrot and four tablespoons of chopped coriander all go in, a litre of boiling water is poured over, and from that moment the lid stays on and the spoon stays out. Stirring rice while it absorbs is what makes it claggy.
ingredients: 1 cm piece fresh ginger, grated fine
2 large red ripe tomatoes, finely chopped
1 bunch fresh coriander — 60 ml (4 tbsp) chopped
Chilli powder, optional — the source prints the range backwards, as 1 1/2 to 1 tsp
300 g chicken breast, bones and skin removed, cubed
// Used in the method but absent from the printed list
equipment: Medium saucepan with a tight lid
steps: Slice the onions. Grate the ginger and garlic on the smallest holes of the grater, and the carrots on the largest. Chop enough coriander to make 4 tablespoons. Peel and cube the potatoes. Finely chop the tomatoes.

Heat the oil in a medium pan and fry the onions until they begin to colour. Add the garlic, ginger, pilau masala, chicken masala, salt and chilli powder if using, and stir briskly on medium heat 2 to 3 minutes.
Add the chicken and cook, stirring, until well browned. Remove the chicken, cover it and set it aside.

In the same pan add the tomatoes and cook, stirring, 1 to 2 minutes. Add the tomato paste and stir another 1 to 2 minutes. Add the potatoes and enough water to form a thick sauce, and cook, stirring occasionally, until fairly dry.
Meanwhile boil 1 litre of water in a kettle or a separate pan.
Add the rice to the potato mixture and stir it well. Return the chicken with the grated carrots and chopped coriander and mix well. The mixture should be quite dry.
Pour in the litre of hot water and bring to the boil. Reduce the heat and cover the pan as soon as it starts simmering.
Add the cooked peas halfway through the cooking.
Keep the pan covered and do not stir at all.
Once the rice is cooked, stir it up to distribute the chicken and vegetables evenly. Serve hot.
chefTips: Do not stir once the water is in. That is the single instruction the recipe puts in its own emphatic terms, and it is why this comes out as separate grains.
Take the chicken out after browning. Left in, breast meat is dry by the time the rice is done.
Cook the potato and tomato mixture until fairly dry before the rice goes in. Wet at that stage and your liquid ratio is wrong.
Boil the litre of water separately and have it ready. Adding cold water stops the cooking and throws the timing.
Grate the garlic and ginger on the smallest holes and the carrots on the largest — the recipe is specific and it is right about both.
Four tablespoons of chopped coriander from the bunch. That is a real amount and it is meant to be.
The chilli powder quantity is printed as a range running backwards, 1½ to 1 teaspoon. It is reproduced as printed; a teaspoon is a sensible reading.
The litre of water appears only in the method, not the ingredient list.
commonMistakes: Stirring after the water goes in.
Adding the rice to a wet tomato mixture.
sources: Adapted from 'Chicken Pilau', Daily Monitor Full Woman, 19 February 2016, updated 6 January 2021, unbylined — all quantities, the grate-fine-and-grate-coarse instructions, the brown-and-remove-the-chicken step, the cook-until-fairly-dry stage, the separately boiled litre of water, the peas halfway through and the emphatic do-not-stir-at-all instruction are all as printed there.

That page prints its chilli powder quantity as a descending range, '1½ -1 tsp', which is reproduced rather than corrected. The 1 litre of water appears in its method only, not in its ingredient list, and '1 bunch fresh coriander' in the list is refined to 4 tablespoons chopped in the method.
reheating: Steam or microwave with a splash of water. Do not stir it while hot.
healthBenefits: Chicken breast is lean, high-protein and rich in niacin and selenium.
Carrots, peas, potato and tomato all go into the same pot.
Two tablespoons of oil across five servings.
Whole-spice masalas rather than a sauce base.
culturalNote: Pilau is function food in Uganda — weddings, graduations, introductions — and everyone has an opinion about it. The two methods in this collection, the absorption one here and the stir-fry in UGA077, are both Ugandan and both published in the same newspaper, which is a good illustration of how a borrowed dish settles into more than one local form.
